slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by separating Euclidean geometry from coordinate bookkeeping. The chapter treats rigid motion as a structural test: distances, angles, orientation, and curve invariants should survive exactly when the theory says they do. Tell students that every visual in the deck has an invariant to inspect, not merely a shape to admire.

slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Use this route slide to give the chapter a spine. The lecture starts with rigid motions in R3, then asks what the derivative of such a motion does to tangent data, and then uses determinant sign to distinguish orientation preserving from orientation reversing maps. The last third turns those ideas into congruence tests for curves.

slides.label: Euclidean Data
slides.notes: The key point is that Euclidean space carries more than a list of coordinates. Coordinates let us calculate, but the metric, inner product, and orientation are the objects a rigid motion must respect. Emphasize that the origin is not sacred: translations move it, while the vector-level inner product remains the measuring device.

slides.label: Rigid Motion Form
slides.notes: This is the algebraic model for the whole chapter. A Euclidean isometry is represented as a translation followed by an orthogonal linear map, so the distance calculation collapses to the identity C transpose C equals I. The displayed tetrahedron is deliberately asymmetric so that students can see the object move without confusing the motion with a symmetry of the object.

slides.label: Distance Witness
slides.notes: Walk through the two-segment measurement in the diagram. The original edge and moved edge have different locations and directions in the drawing, but their lengths agree because the orthogonal part preserves dot products. This is the first example of a visual paired with a numerical witness.

slides.label: Tangent Map
slides.notes: For a general smooth map, the derivative can depend on the base point. For a rigid motion F(p)=a+Cp, the tangent map is unusually clean: every tangent vector is carried by the same matrix C, regardless of where it is attached. This is why rigid motions preserve not just distances between points, but the entire first-order measuring apparatus.

slides.label: Frames
slides.notes: A frame is a portable measuring instrument: three unit directions, mutually perpendicular, attached to a point. Under an orientation-preserving rigid motion, the frame remains right handed; under a reflection, it becomes left handed. The diagram turns the determinant sign into a visible handedness test.

slides.label: Orientation Test
slides.notes: This slide turns orientation into a computation. The determinant of the matrix with columns u, v, w equals the triple scalar product, so its sign records which side of the plane the third vector occupies. A rigid motion with determinant plus one preserves this sign, while determinant minus one reverses it.

slides.label: Orthogonal Group
slides.notes: Pause here to classify the linear part before returning to geometry. Orthogonal matrices split into two components according to determinant sign, and the translation vector then places the motion in space. This separation keeps the algebra small while retaining the geometric consequences.

slides.label: Reflection Dashboard
slides.notes: Use the dashboard as a diagnostic example rather than a list of formulas. A reflection preserves distances and angles but reverses orientation, so it is an isometry with determinant minus one. Students should learn to read the sign, not the visual style, as the orientation certificate.

slides.label: Euclidean Geometry as Invariants
slides.notes: This slide connects the chapter back to the broader course. Euclidean geometry studies the properties that remain unchanged under rigid motions: length, angle, orthogonality, curvature of curves, and torsion up to the appropriate orientation convention. Coordinates are useful only to the extent that they expose those invariants cleanly.

slides.label: Curves Under Motion
slides.notes: A curve moved by a rigid motion has velocity, speed, and curvature transformed in predictable ways. Translation disappears under differentiation, and the orthogonal matrix preserves vector norms. The result is that the shape data of a curve is unchanged, even when the curve is relocated and rotated in space.

slides.label: Helix Certificate
slides.notes: The helix is a compact test case because both curvature and torsion are visible but not trivial. A proper rotation keeps the full Frenet data consistent, while a reflection keeps curvature and reverses the orientation-dependent sign of torsion. The deck uses this as the curve-level analogue of determinant sign.

slides.label: Congruence Strategy
slides.notes: Present congruence as an evidence chain. If two curves have matching curvature and torsion data on corresponding parameter intervals, one tries to build the rigid motion that aligns an initial frame and then propagates the Frenet equations. The theorem is not being quoted here; it is being turned into an operational proof plan.

slides.label: Applied Lab
slides.notes: The applied lab mirrors the notebook's validation habit. Students choose one parameter or one transformation, predict which invariant should remain stable, rerun or mentally recompute the witness, and check whether the residual agrees. The goal is to make failures informative rather than mysterious.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by returning to the three recurring habits. First, rigid motions are algebraic enough to compute but geometric enough to classify. Second, tangent maps and frames turn motion into local measurement. Third, curve congruence becomes practical when curvature, torsion, and orientation are treated as data with checks attached.
